How this campaign works

You play a Roman sent ahead of the main force — a legionary officer, a camp scribe, a camp cook, a praetor, or a consul, drawn at random each time you start or restart a campaign, with a name and a portrait to match. Whoever you are this time, the whole theater is on the map at once and you always see exactly where the enemy is — nothing is hidden. What moves is you, and what moves against you is the enemy force named in the briefing. Both of your starting positions are also drawn fresh from a pool of plausible spots every time, so the map layout you're looking at, and the safe route through it, won't be the same twice.

Reading the map: every city is shown as a dot with its name labeled, just like the source DARE webmap. When two names would overlap at the current zoom, the less important one steps aside — but you, the enemy, both objectives, and anywhere you can march to this turn are always labeled no matter how tight the map gets. Your own objective gets a pulsing 🏁 ring so it's never in doubt which city you're actually racing toward. A blue ring means you can click that city to march there this turn. Use the theater/world toggle (top-left) or the target/grid buttons (top-right) to switch between this campaign's default zoomed-in view and the entire map. The most important thing that just happened is always posted as a banner across the top of the screen, right under the title bar — the sidebar log underneath keeps the full turn-by-turn history if you want to scroll back through it. Every road you've actually marched down stays traced on the map in a small brown trail, each stop numbered by the turn you reached it, so you can always see your own route through the theater at a glance, the way a real campaign map would mark it.

Turns and marching: click any city on the map, not just a next-door one, and you march immediately — there's no preview step that tells you the turn cost before you've committed to anything. If it's one road away, that's the whole turn. If it's further, the game runs the same breadth-first search (BFS) the enemy uses to plot the shortest known road route there, highlights it in blue, and marches the first leg right away; the enemy takes its real turn, and only then does it stop and ask whether to continue onto the next leg or stop where you are. Every hop plays out fully before the next is offered — you move, the enemy responds, you see exactly where it is — so you're always deciding with current information, never with a full turn-by-turn itinerary laid out in advance. The only way to find out how long a road actually is is to start marching it. Routes are now genuinely long: real roads that used to be a single click are broken up into their actual real waypoint towns along the way, and most campaigns now take well over a dozen real turns to complete, so a march across a theater is a real multi-turn journey full of real decision points, not one hop.

The enemy moves too, using the same shortest-path search (breadth-first search, BFS) throughout: at first it marches toward its own fixed objective by the shortest route, recomputed fresh every turn, and does not know or care where you are. But it is also checking, every turn, its own BFS distance to you. Come within 6 roads of it and it abandons its march entirely, switching permanently to hunting: from then on its shortest path is recalculated against your current position instead of its old objective, every single turn, so it adapts immediately to wherever you go next. Once it's hunting you, it never goes back to its old plan. The topbar flags this in red (⚔ HUNTING YOU) the moment it happens.

Where the actual decisions are: the road network has real branching — most cities have three or more viable ways in or out, not one forced corridor, and the real waypoint towns that break up long roads are cross-linked to their neighbors on other nearby roads too, not just strung along a single dead-straight line — so the shortest BFS route to your objective is rarely the only sane one, and it's often not the safest. The whole map is one connected road network, so wherever you end up, some route to your objective always exists; the only real cost of a detour is the turns it spends. The enemy's route is just as visible to you as yours is to it: a dashed amber line traces its own live BFS path across the map at all times, recalculated fresh every turn from wherever it actually is — toward its objective normally, or straight at you the instant it starts hunting, when the line itself flares bright magenta and pulses faster. Watch that line shift in real time as you move, and choose a longer route that keeps you further from its path (and further than its detection radius) instead of blindly taking the fastest one. Since the starting layout is randomized every game, there's no single memorized route that always works.

Winning: reach your objective city before the enemy reaches theirs, and before the enemy ever occupies the same city as you.

Losing: the enemy reaches its objective first (their goal is secured on schedule, the way it may have happened historically), the enemy catches you by ending up on your city (far more likely once it's hunting you), or you run out of turns.

Every city on this map is a real place from the Digital Atlas of the Roman Empire (DARE, dare.ht.lu.se), the academic gazetteer behind the klokantech/roman-empire map project; 494 of the 504 cities use DARE's own surveyed coordinates directly, and the rest (a lake, a mountain pass, a river crossing, a stretch of open border country) are reconstructed because DARE doesn't carry a point for them. 398 of those 504 are waypoint towns added on top of the historical hub cities: 208 string out the longer roads between hubs, and a further 190 are real nearby places branched in specifically wherever a stretch would otherwise have been a forced single-file corridor with nothing else around to cross-link to — each one kept a real distance from its neighbors so the map stays readable rather than cluttered.

Roads work the same way: where DARE's own road-segment data (roads_low.geojson from that project) actually links two cities, this map draws that real, attested road, traced point for point. Where no single attested segment connects two cities directly — a common gap, since DARE only records roads that have actually been surveyed or excavated, not a hypothetical complete network — the map falls back to a dashed straight line between them, clearly marked as reconstructed rather than attested. Hover any road to see which kind it is. 618 of this map's 903 roads are directly attested; 285 are reconstructed gaps.
